source.title: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Language Models
source.authors: Yifei He; Alon Benhaim; Barun Patra; Praneetha Vaddamanu; Sanchit Ahuja; Parul Chopra; Vishrav Chaudhary; Han Zhao; Xia Song

record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law scaling and loss prediction in multilingual decoder-only pretraining, extending scaling-law analysis to a new training setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fitted loss curves, joint scaling-law fits, held-out prediction results, and multilingual sampling-ratio experiments. Results cited from prior scaling-law work are not recorded as findings. The sampling-ratio optimization is distinct from compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study trains 100+ multilingual decoder-only LMs (85M–1.2B non-embedding parameters, 25B–100B tokens). It fits test loss as power laws in the family sampling ratio, model size and dataset size, using a Chinchilla-form joint law. It then checks the fit's prediction on held-out low-loss points. This is a new data setting (multilingual mixtures) for the text-pretraining loss law, but it covers only about one order of magnitude in N and less in D.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that each family's test loss follows a power law in model size, dataset size and its own sampling ratio, independent of other families. They also conclude that optimal ratios from 85M models transfer to 1.2B models. The authors call 85M→1.2B 'several orders of magnitude', but it is about 14x, i.e. roughly one order.
record.recipe_differences: The study builds a multilingual decoder-only pretraining law with an additional language-family sampling-ratio term and tests family-level transfer. It uses a Chinchilla-style model/data form as part of the proposed joint law rather than reproducing the original monolingual scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that family loss depends on its own sampling ratio when grouped by language family, but varies when linguistically related Indic languages are split across random groups. It also states that the proposed formulation is less useful for very small N, D and p, including p=0.

fits_no_version.finding: With a family's ratio held fixed, its loss barely changes as other families' ratios vary. Randomly split Indic groups show cross-group transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-family loss in multilingual pretraining depends mainly on that family's own sampling ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Sampling ratios optimised at 85M give 1.2B total loss 9.104, against 9.101 for ratios optimised at 1.2B. Both beat the baselines (9.108–9.236).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal multilingual mixture ratios transfer from small to larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: The sampling-ratio exponent γ is invariant to N and D (parallel log-log lines).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-mixture exponents are scale-invariant in multilingual pretraining.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study tests multilingual family-level scaling, not the full monolingual claim across compute scales. The held-out prediction result gives no numerical error and is not a small-run-only test of loss prediction on much larger runs. The paper itself notes limitations at very small N, D and p, including the p=0 case. Standard deviations are shown for some mixture experiments, but uncertainty for the fitted scaling-law parameters is not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Did not record every individual baseline mixture result in Tables 3-6; those comparisons concern language-family sampling-ratio optimization rather than any listed claim version. Included the larger-model transfer result in r37-r38 as a finding outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: Compute as the variable. Ranges of several orders of magnitude (N spans ~14x, D ~4x).
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger from small-run fits. A quantitative prediction error.
All of it: no parameter/token split at fixed compute.
All of it: shape co-varies with size.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Multilingual text pretraining is treated under V1.
All of it: no downstream tasks.
Fitting method, parameter counting and schedule choices. Only data (language family) dependence is shown.

missing.what: Loss vs N at fixed D (85M–1.2B) is linear in log-log for each p. Loss vs D at fixed N=85M (25B–100B) is also linear. These are the direct V1 power-law-in-N/D evidence.
γ is invariant across N and D (parallel log L vs log p lines).
Joint-law fits at 100B tokens and per-family joint fits.

record.verdict_notes: The V5 links are removed: multilingual text pretraining is treated as a text-pretraining setting under V1. There is no uncertainty on the fitted parameters. The limitations section notes the law breaks at p=0 and may fail for small N, D and p. That is stated, not measured.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model size and dataset size scaling in multilingual pretraining, as well as language-family sampling-ratio fits. Does not directly test training compute as the independent scaling variable or establish the monolingual claim across several orders of magnitude.

Reports held-out loss prediction on the lower 20% of loss data and transfer of sampling ratios from 85M to 1.2B parameters. Does not report a direct test where a power law fitted only on small runs predicts the held-out loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The paper optimizes language-family sampling ratios, not the parameter-count/token-count split at a fixed compute budget.
Model configurations vary with model size; the paper does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count.
Tests multilingual text pretraining only. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not systematically vary fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or datasets to test how they change the fitted laws.
